Prompt wording could be read as splitting implicit and limited, but this pass retains the existing local three-value pilot authority.

comparator_clusters.rationale: Graph-based neighborhood encoders for domain calling, mainly without required morphology.

comparator_clusters.cluster_name: Cluster B: Image-informed graph and multimodal domain callers
comparator_clusters.rationale: Morphology or image-augmented integration is central or decision-relevant.

comparator_clusters.cluster_name: Cluster C: Bayesian, probabilistic, and latent-model domain callers
comparator_clusters.rationale: Domains emerge from Bayesian smoothing, probabilistic alignment, or spatially structured embedding.

comparator_clusters.cluster_name: Cluster D: Multiscale and tissue-architecture structure methods
comparator_clusters.rationale: Emphasize multiscale context, tissue architecture, slice structure, or scalable structural segmentation-style domain discovery.

comparator_clusters.cluster_name: Cluster E: Topic, semantic, and interpretable domain discovery
comparator_clusters.rationale: Domains are mediated by semantic priors, interpretable topics, gene programs, or pattern modules.
Nearest comparators bridge multiple clusters rather than fitting one clean family.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates
rows.Main Use in This Topic: spatial domain identification through neighbor-augmented clustering
rows.Key Difference: Uses a neighbor-augmented product space and neighborhood gradients for domain calling rather than deep graph encoders or Bayesian smoothing.
rows.Evidence Note: Method paper explicitly supports spatial domain segmentation with multiscale neighborhood features. Comparator fields and burden cues remain Layer 2 pilot judgment.
rows.Best First Choice When: When you want scalable spatial clustering driven by local neighborhood transcriptome without committing to heavier deep multimodal models.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When explicit joint multi-slice modeling or image-guided domain calling is the first-order requirement.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates across sections
rows.Main Use in This Topic: joint spatial domain identification with cell-type composition modeling
rows.Key Difference: Jointly models cell types and spatial domains in a Bayesian hierarchical multi-sample framework rather than only smoothing spot labels or learning deep graph embeddings.
rows.Evidence Note: Benchmark and review coverage support BASS as a Bayesian multi-sample domain method. Comparator fields and burden cues remain Layer 2 pilot judgment.
rows.Main Spatial Prior: Bayesian spatial smoothing + hierarchical multi-sample modeling
rows.Best First Choice When: When joint analysis across multiple sections matters and you want spatial domains tied to cell-type composition structure.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When you only need a light single-slice baseline or want image-aware domain calling instead of hierarchical multi-sample modeling.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates
rows.Main Use in This Topic: single-slice Bayesian spatial domain identification
rows.Key Difference: Prioritizes Bayesian spatial smoothing for single-slice domain calling rather than multi-sample alignment or deep graph representation learning.
rows.Evidence Note: Benchmark and review coverage support BayesSpace as a single-slice Bayesian domain baseline. Multi-slice and burden cues remain conservative Layer 2 judgment.
rows.Best First Choice When: When you want a stable Bayesian single-slice baseline for spot-based domain calling.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When joint multi-slice integration, reference guidance, or morphology-aware deep models are the main need.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates
rows.Main Use in This Topic: graph-based spatial domain identification from spatial clustering
rows.Key Difference: Uses graph convolution for spatial clustering without iterative imputation, continuity-focused embedding, or image-aware contrastive fusion.
rows.Evidence Note: Benchmark and review coverage support CCST as a graph-based spatial clustering method for domain calling. Comparator fields and burden cues remain Layer 2 pilot judgment.
rows.Best First Choice When: When you want a straightforward graph-convolution comparator without morphology or multi-slice alignment.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When image-aware modeling, explicit batch correction, or stronger modern graph baselines are the first-order requirement.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates
rows.Main Use in This Topic: robust spatial domain identification with iterative graph-embedding refinement
rows.Key Difference: Uses DEG selection and imputation to stabilize graph-based domain calling rather than relying only on one-pass graph embedding or contrastive training.
rows.Evidence Note: Genome Biology 2024 places ADEPT inside the spatial clustering benchmark set and ranks it among the top tools across main recommendation scenarios. Cross-slice, burden, and comparator fields remain Layer 2 pilot provisional judgment, and one large-slice memory limitation is noted in the benchmark.
rows.Best First Choice When: When you want a morphology-free deep clustering method that explicitly prioritizes robustness to noisy or uneven ST data quality.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When explicit joint multi-slice integration, image-aware modeling, or a clearly scalability-first method is the first-order requirement.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates
rows.Main Use in This Topic: joint embedding-and-clustering spatial domain identification
rows.Key Difference: Couples low-dimensional embedding learning with spatial clustering in one model rather than adding Bayesian smoothing after reduction or aligning multiple slides jointly.
rows.Evidence Note: Benchmark and review coverage support DR-SC as a joint embedding-and-clustering domain method. Burden and scale cues remain conservative Layer 2 judgment.
rows.Best First Choice When: When you want a CPU-oriented method that learns spatial embedding and domain labels together for a single slice.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When multi-slice alignment, morphology input, or explicit reference guidance is central to the problem.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates + histology image
rows.Main Use in This Topic: spatial domain identification with morphology-aware deep integration
rows.Key Difference: Uses deep morphology-aware fusion with domain-adversarial integration rather than histology-guided contrastive learning, image-guided graph construction, or lighter optional-image models.
rows.Evidence Note: Method paper explicitly supports morphology-aware spatial domain identification and batch integration. Cross-slice routine use remains a conservative Layer 2 judgment.
rows.Best First Choice When: When histology is informative and cross-batch or cross-technology integration is part of the domain-calling problem.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When you want a lighter single-slice baseline or do not want to rely on deep multimodal training.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates + histology image
rows.Main Use in This Topic: spatial domain identification with histology-guided contrastive integration
rows.Key Difference: Uses cross-modal contrastive learning to adapt gene expression to histology rather than using image signal only for graph construction, weighting, or transformer-style fusion.
rows.Evidence Note: Genome Biology 2024 explicitly positions ConGI as a clustering/domain method and highlights it as especially effective on tumor datasets. Non-tumor generality, comparator fields, and burden cues remain Layer 2 pilot provisional judgment.
rows.Main Spatial Prior: deep multimodal fusion + contrastive histology coupling
rows.Best First Choice When: When histology is central to the domain boundary and the dataset is pathology- or tumor-oriented rather than a generic morphology-light tissue slice.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When histology is unavailable, weakly informative, or you need a morphology-free or multi-slice batch-aware baseline first.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates
rows.Main Use in This Topic: spatial domain identification with graph self-supervised embeddings
rows.Key Difference: Uses self-supervised contrastive graph representation with explicit joint-slice integration and batch correction rather than iterative imputation, attention weighting, or optional-morphology multimodal fusion.
rows.Evidence Note: Method paper explicitly supports graph-based domain calling with joint-slice integration and batch correction. Comparator fields and burden cues remain Layer 2 pilot judgment.
rows.Best First Choice When: When you want a modern graph-based core method that also supports joint slice integration with batch correction.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When morphology is central or you only need a simple CPU Bayesian baseline.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates + optional histology image
rows.Main Use in This Topic: spatial domain identification with multimodal contrastive graph embedding
rows.Key Difference: Uses one contrastive framework that can integrate morphology when available without making image signal mandatory, unlike graph-only or image-central alternatives.
rows.Evidence Note: Genome Biology 2024 explicitly places conST inside the spatial clustering benchmark set as a multimodal contrastive framework for domain-relevant clustering. Comparator fields and burden cues remain Layer 2 pilot provisional judgment.
rows.Main Spatial Prior: deep multimodal fusion + contrastive graph embedding
rows.Best First Choice When: When you want a single contrastive spatial-domain model that can use morphology if available but does not require an image-first workflow.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When you need either a cleaner graph-only baseline or a more explicitly image-driven domain model as the first choice.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates across slices
rows.Main Use in This Topic: multi-range tissue-structure spatial domain identification
rows.Key Difference: Builds domains from explicit multi-range cellular-context representation rather than deep graph or image models or Bayesian spot smoothing.
rows.Evidence Note: Method paper explicitly supports scalable tissue-structure domain identification with multi-slice alignment. Comparator fields and burden cues remain Layer 2 pilot judgment.
rows.Best First Choice When: When you need fast scalable structure identification across multiple slices without relying on image features.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When histology-driven boundaries or explicit batch-aware latent integration is the first-order need.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates across slides
rows.Main Use in This Topic: joint spatial domain identification with multi-slide alignment
rows.Key Difference: Simultaneously aligns embeddings and domain labels across slides with a probabilistic integration model rather than only smoothing single-slice labels or using deep graph encoders.
rows.Evidence Note: Method paper explicitly supports joint embedding alignment and domain identification across slides. Burden cues and comparator fields remain Layer 2 pilot judgment.
rows.Main Spatial Prior: latent embedding + aligned spatial factor model
rows.Best First Choice When: When multi-slide integration with batch effects is central and you want a probabilistic alignment-based domain method.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When you only need a simple single-slice domain baseline or image-aware domain calling.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates
rows.Main Use in This Topic: spatial domain identification coupled to spatial pattern discovery
rows.Key Difference: Couples domain calling to quantitative spatial-pattern and SVG scoring rather than using graph encoders or pure topic models alone.
rows.Evidence Note: Method paper explicitly supports spatial pattern discovery with domain detection. Its topic placement and comparator fields remain Layer 2 judgment.
rows.Best First Choice When: When you want domain identification tied closely to spatial pattern discovery rather than only a standalone clustering output.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When explicit multi-slice integration, marker/reference guidance, or a cleaner pure-domain baseline is the main need.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates + marker genes
rows.Main Use in This Topic: marker-guided semantic spatial domain annotation
rows.Key Difference: Uses marker-guided Bayesian semantic annotation to produce domain labels with biological semantics rather than de novo graph clustering or purely unsupervised topic-domain discovery.
rows.Evidence Note: Method paper explicitly supports marker-guided Bayesian semantic annotation on spatial data. Its placement under domain identification and the abstraction of its semantic outputs to domain labels remain Layer 2 pilot judgment.
rows.Best First Choice When: When informative marker knowledge already exists and you want biologically named spatial semantics rather than purely de novo clusters.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When you need a fully unsupervised domain caller without marker priors.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates
rows.Main Use in This Topic: spatial domain identification through deep spatial embedding
rows.Key Difference: Uses deep latent embedding with variational graph autoencoding rather than attention-based graph models, self-supervised contrastive integration, or iterative imputation-driven clustering.
rows.Evidence Note: Benchmark and review coverage support SEDR as a deep spatial embedding method for domain calling. Burden and scale cues remain conservative Layer 2 judgment.
rows.Best First Choice When: When you want a deep spatial embedding model that stays useful for clustering and follow-on correction or denoising tasks.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When explicit image integration or a fully Bayesian multi-sample domain model is the main need.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates across adjacent slices
rows.Main Use in This Topic: cross-slice coherent spatial domain identification
rows.Key Difference: Focuses on domains coherent across adjacent slices and 3D architecture reconstruction rather than single-slice clustering or Bayesian smoothing.
rows.Evidence Note: Method paper explicitly supports cross-slice coherent spatial domains and 3D architecture alignment. This row emphasizes the domain module rather than the full toolkit surface.
rows.Best First Choice When: When cross-slice coherent domains and downstream 3D tissue architecture are central to the question.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When you only need a lightweight single-slice baseline or explicit reference-guided semantics.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates
rows.Main Use in This Topic: spatial domain identification with continuity-sensitive graph embedding
rows.Key Difference: Uses spatially regularized graph embedding to favor continuous and coherent domain boundaries rather than attention weighting, multiscale feature augmentation, or batch-aware contrastive integration.
rows.Evidence Note: Method paper and PubMed record explicitly support domain segmentation, while Genome Biology 2024 and SRTBenchmark support SpaceFlow as a continuity-sensitive clustering method. Cross-slice and batch fields remain Layer 2 pilot provisional judgment because the public evidence is much stronger on continuity and segmentation than on multi-slice or batch semantics.
rows.Main Spatial Prior: graph neighborhood + spatially regularized latent embedding
rows.Best First Choice When: When you need morphology-free domain calling with especially strong spatial continuity on high-resolution or high-continuity tissue structure.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the main objective is explicit batch-aware joint multi-slice integration rather than continuity-sensitive single-slice segmentation.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates
rows.Main Use in This Topic: graph-attention spatial domain identification
rows.Key Difference: Uses adaptive attention on neighborhood edges rather than contrastive learning, iterative imputation, or continuity-focused embedding.
rows.Evidence Note: Method paper explicitly supports graph-attention domain calling with consecutive-section extension. Burden cues and comparator fields remain Layer 2 judgment.
rows.Best First Choice When: When you want a strong graph-based baseline with adaptive neighborhood weighting and possible consecutive-section extension.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When morphology or explicit batch-aware integration is more central than graph attention itself.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates
rows.Main Use in This Topic: interpretable spatial topic discovery for tissue domains
rows.Key Difference: Uses interpretable spatial topics and gene modules to support tissue-domain identification rather than directly optimizing only discrete graph clusters or Bayesian spot labels.
rows.Evidence Note: Method paper explicitly supports spatial topics and gene modules aligned with tissue domains. The reduction of these outputs to domain labels for this topic remains a Layer 2 pilot judgment.
rows.Best First Choice When: When interpretability and topic-level biological structure matter as much as the domain partition itself.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When you need a direct discrete domain caller without topic-to-domain interpretation.

rows.Main Input: baseline cluster labels + ST matrix + spatial coordinates
rows.Main Use in This Topic: post-processing / consensus spatial domain identification from multiple baseline methods
rows.Key Difference: Aggregates multiple baseline domain calls into a consensus result rather than learning a single latent spatial model itself.
rows.Evidence Note: Method paper explicitly supports consensus domain detection from multiple baseline methods. In this topic it is retained as a post-processing / consensus method rather than a typical standalone first-pass domain model, and several selection fields remain pilot provisional Layer 2 judgment.
rows.Best First Choice When: When you want to stabilize domain calls by reconciling several strong baseline methods on the same dataset.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When you need a standalone first-pass model without running or choosing baseline methods first.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates + multichannel image
rows.Main Use in This Topic: spatial domain identification with image-augmented graph transformer
rows.Key Difference: Makes multichannel image features central in a graph-transformer architecture rather than using histology-guided contrastive learning or lighter optional-image graph weighting.
rows.Evidence Note: Method paper explicitly supports image-augmented graph-transformer domain identification. Burden cues and comparator fields remain Layer 2 pilot judgment.
rows.Main Spatial Prior: deep multimodal fusion + image-augmented graph transformer
rows.Best First Choice When: When rich multichannel imaging is available and morphology should drive domain delineation rather than just refine it.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When histology is absent or you want a graph baseline that can operate without image features.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates + histology image
rows.Main Use in This Topic: spatial domain identification with histology-aware graph construction
rows.Key Difference: Uses histology-informed graph construction for domain calling unlike graph-only alternatives, image-required contrastive models, or heavier multimodal fusion approaches.
rows.Evidence Note: Method paper explicitly supports histology-aware domain calling from expression and coordinates. Comparator fields, cross-slice/batch cues, and burden cues remain Layer 2 pilot provisional judgment.
rows.Best First Choice When: When histology is available or likely informative and you want an established within-slice histology-aware graph baseline.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When explicit batch-aware correction or native joint multi-slice modeling is the first-order requirement.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates across sections
rows.Main Use in This Topic: efficient multi-section spatial domain identification
rows.Key Difference: Uses an efficient convolutional formulation over image-like spatial tensors rather than graph encoders or Bayesian smoothing, with built-in adjacent-section alignment.
rows.Evidence Note: Method paper explicitly supports efficient CNN-based spatial domain identification with adjacent-section alignment. Comparator fields and burden cues remain Layer 2 pilot judgment.
rows.Best First Choice When: When you want efficient domain identification that can also align adjacent sections without relying on image morphology or external references.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When you need a simple CPU baseline or explicit marker or reference-guided domain semantics.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates + matched scRNA reference
rows.Main Use in This Topic: topic-based pathology-relevant spatial domain identification
rows.Key Difference: Uses topic modeling over deconvolution-informed cluster structure to recover pathology-relevant domains rather than purely de novo graph or Bayesian clustering.
rows.Evidence Note: Method paper explicitly supports pathology-relevant spatial domains from matched single-cell and spatial data. External-guidance interpretation remains a Layer 2 judgment.
rows.Best First Choice When: When matched scRNA information is available and you care about pathology-relevant domains defined by coherent cell-type organization.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When you need fully unsupervised domain calling without reference information.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates
rows.Main Use in This Topic: spatial domain identification through spatially aware dimension reduction
rows.Key Difference: Learns spatially aware low-dimensional components that can be paired with downstream clustering rather than directly using graph encoders or hierarchical Bayesian domain models.
rows.Evidence Note: Benchmark and review coverage support SpatialPCA as a spatial embedding baseline for domain detection. Burden cues remain Layer 2 judgment.
rows.Best First Choice When: When you want a CPU-oriented spatial embedding baseline that can support domain detection and related downstream structure analyses.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When explicit multi-slice integration, image input, or direct semantic guidance is the first-order need.

rows.Method Family: Spatially aware deconvolution and domain identification
rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates
rows.Main Use in This Topic: fast spatial domain identification with local microenvironment weighting
rows.Key Difference: Uses local microenvironment weighted expression for fast domain calling rather than consensus aggregation or heavier continuity-sensitive and graph-contrastive models.
rows.Evidence Note: Method paper and official docs explicitly support a clustering path that uses expression and spatial locations only. Its closest-alternative and related selection cues remain pilot provisional Layer 2 judgment.
rows.Best First Choice When: When you want a very fast first-pass spatial domain call on a large spot dataset without relying on image input.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When joint multi-slice alignment, topic interpretability, or a standalone consensus workflow is more important than fast local microenvironment clustering.

rows.Main Input: ST matrix + spatial coordinates + optional histology image
rows.Main Use in This Topic: SME-corrected graph-based spatial domain identification
rows.Key Difference: Uses SME-style integration of morphology, distance, and expression in a broad downstream toolkit rather than an image-required contrastive model or a dedicated domain-only deep integration workflow.
rows.Evidence Note: Method paper and official docs explicitly support SME-based clustering with optional morphology. Comparator fields and domain-only positioning remain Layer 2 judgment.
rows.Best First Choice When: When you want a flexible toolkit that can use morphology if available but still operate without it for spatial clustering and downstream exploration.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When you need explicit multi-slice integration or a dedicated domain-only model with stronger alignment machinery.

fields_least_stable: Do Not Start With This When
pilot_issues: Batch Handling wording drift is real: current local authority uses implicit / limited as one value, and that stayed workable, but future readers may want the split made explicit.
Cross-slice Support and Batch Handling are related but not interchangeable; this topic repeatedly pushed toward conflating them.
Closest Alternatives and Key Difference remain usable, but boundary rows such as STCC and SpatialPrompt make it clear that these local-comparison fields should still be treated as pilot provisional.
schema_pressure_test.readiness_assessment: This schema is good enough to support the next domain-identification iteration. The strongest support comes from the combination of frozen shared fields, topic-specific structural cues, and comparator clusters, but burden fields plus Closest Alternatives, Key Difference, Cross-slice Support, and Batch Handling should still be treated as pilot-level rather than final policy.
